question: What is the primary purpose of a runbook?
options: To give on-call responders clear, step-by-step guidance for diagnosing and resolving a specific alert or failure
To record employee vacation schedules
To replace all monitoring dashboards
To store the source code of the pipeline
explanation: A runbook documents concrete steps to triage and remediate a known problem, reducing time-to-resolution and dependence on tribal knowledge during an incident.

question: Which practice most improves a healthy on-call rotation?
options: Assigning one person to be on-call permanently with no breaks
Sustainable rotations, clear escalation paths, and actionable alerts tied to runbooks
Paging the whole company for every warning
Removing all alerts to avoid waking anyone
explanation: Good on-call relies on sustainable rotations that avoid burnout, defined escalation, and alerts that are actionable and linked to runbooks so responders know what to do.

question: An alert fires but has no linked runbook and the responder has never seen it. What is the best follow-up?
options: Delete the alert so it never fires again
Ignore it since it resolved itself
After resolving, write or link a runbook and improve the alert so future responders are prepared
Escalate every future occurrence directly to the CEO
explanation: Missing runbooks are a gap to close: document the diagnosis and fix so the next responder is equipped. This is part of continuously improving on-call quality.

question: What distinguishes a page-worthy alert from an informational one?
options: Page-worthy alerts are cheaper to send
Page-worthy alerts require immediate human action to prevent or stop customer impact; informational ones do not
Informational alerts always indicate outages
There is no difference; everything should page
explanation: Only conditions needing urgent human intervention should page. Non-urgent signals belong in tickets or dashboards to avoid alert fatigue and burnout.

question: Why should a runbook be tested or reviewed periodically?
options: Because runbooks expire automatically after a week
Because auditors require exactly weekly reviews by law
Because systems change, and stale runbook steps can mislead responders during a real incident
Runbooks never need review once written
explanation: Pipelines and infrastructure evolve, so runbook steps can become outdated. Periodic review (and drills) keeps them accurate and trustworthy under pressure.
